build: Softrambo and The Wanderer Group D64

exclude: CPU port, runtime zero-page pointers and counters, and scratch left by the loader
KERNAL work area and final depacker relocated from $08D0 by $081D
Boot screen and the old VIC-bank sprite pointers touched at $0A1B and $0A1E
Working copy of the current round event seed, loaded by $0ACA
Runtime sprite records, status arrays, active object queue and mirror cache initialised at $0AA8 and $0ADC
Runtime panel and playfield populated by $0A55, $0A68 and the terrain renderer
Hardware sprite pointer cells overwritten by $1FDD and $25AA
Generated terrain or panel glyph destination built by $11AA and $17C6 from the counted source banks
Runtime SID voice records and player registers set by $8000 and $8A6F
Runtime effect record and frequency accumulators set by $86D0
Runtime sprite reversal and opacity tables generated at $2436
Hardware vector words written at $0E44 through $0E59, which overlay the end of the fourth terrain glyph set

comments.text: Enter the expanded game at the jump to $0976 following the release's last depacker.
A selects one of 25 screen rows. Set $04/$05 to its screen RAM address and $06/$07 to its matching colour RAM address, using the three parallel tables at $092B, $0944 and $095D.
Alternate entry following TAX. Use the screen row already in X and fill both pairs of destination pointers.
Low bytes for the 25 rows of the 40-column screen at $4400 and for the corresponding colour cells.
Screen RAM page of each row at $4400 plus 40 times the row number.
Colour RAM page of each row at $D800 plus 40 times the row number.

Initialise the hardware and round state, clear the playfield, copy the lettering set, reset the SID, and run the title and prologue. Initialise again before setting up the player and entering the main loop.

Reset round and input state, expose I/O with the KERNAL banked out, select the VIC bank at $4000 and initialise its raster interrupts, sprites and panel. Install the round's palette, terrain and sprite seed records.
Fetch eight initial queue entries for this round and copy them to $43E0 in reverse order. Then copy the round's 80 event bytes from the address at $0C7D into the working event buffer.
Clear the sprite records and per-object status arrays. Seed the two player records from $0C59, reset player pose and direction, and mark cached flipped shapes stale.

Alternate player and enemy updates under the two raster countdowns at $23 and $24. The first pass handles controls, scrolling, pickup interaction and the player's own state. The second updates active objects, mirrored sprites and collisions. Use the round transition handler while $57 is set.
Apply horizontal increments in object records 8 to 13 during a raster interrupt, unless paused. Restore Y, X and A from the IRQ scratch bytes and return to the interrupted instruction.
Toggle alternating shape frames for slots 0 to 3. Inspect the map next to each slot via $26BF, then flip the horizontal direction when the selected cell is below $20.
Saved slot ordinal while $26BF computes the neighbouring landscape cell.
Choose the ground probe on the right or left of the sprite according to the direction flag.
The two eight-byte sprite records copied to slots 14 and 15, starting at $4370. Their Y coordinate is $9C and the two shape bytes are $33 and $A4.
Sixteen little-endian addresses, each pointing to 80 per-column event bytes copied to $2B8B when that round initialises.
High byte of the first event seed address. The round index doubled selects the later high bytes.
Read the sound mode in $6F. Start the queued effect through $86D0 when the mode permits it, and issue a pending tune through $8000 unless the active cue has already started.
Consume the pending extra-life flag at $4B, increment lives, and redraw the life icons.
When the counter reaches seven, clear it, queue the bonus display and sound, and add 35,000 points to the score twice.
When all five low power bits are set and the bonus has not already been awarded, add four lots of 40,000 points and queue the related panel message.
Saved timer-enable state while the F1 handler waits for a fresh keypress.
Scan the F1 matrix row and column. Stop horizontal scrolling, suppress the timer, set the pause flag, and wait for a release, press and release of F1 before restoring the timer flag.
Scan F3 through CIA1. On press, clear active sprites and scrolling before jumping to the game-over path.
Consume the pending flag at $5C. Add two to the second displayed timer digit and carry into the first when the character code reaches $78.
On the first pressed scan of F5, advance the mode modulo four and start cue zero or cue four according to its low bit. Further scans of the held key leave the mode alone until release.
Decrement $5D if it is nonzero, leaving the elapsed state pinned at zero.
Cached VIC control byte, including the fine horizontal scroll in the low three bits.
Background colour installed at the first landscape raster phase.
Background colour installed near the bottom of the landscape, before the lower panel.
Requests a second driver update after an entire screen column moves.
Nonzero suppresses the main countdown work for the raster.
Set the hardware IRQ vector to $0E84 and the NMI and RESET vectors to $0F9C. Enable raster interrupts, clear the high raster compare bit, select line $D0 and disable CIA1 Timer A interrupts.
Save A, X and Y, acknowledge the raster IRQ, and dispatch on the beam position. Four phases update the playfield, draw edge columns, scan controls and install the lower panel's static character set.
Restore the black panel and its shared colours, eight-pixel text alignment and $7800 glyphs. Update sprites and save the hardware sprite collision bits before servicing scroll or audio.
Install the lower landscape palette, sample controls, adjust the horizontal position of active sprites with the scroll, and update the timer before selecting the lower-panel raster phase.
Set the playfield palette and fine scroll, switch to the glyphs at $7000, and write the sprite registers. Draw a pending edge column, decrement the two main-loop countdowns, then schedule line $90.
Acknowledge CIA1 and restore the three registers saved by the IRQ entry before RTI.
Mark the IRQ motion phase active, save Y, X and A to $2D, $2C and $2F, and permit further raster IRQs while $0B8C adjusts object positions.
Return immediately from the NMI using RTI.
Bank the KERNAL back in and jump to its reset entry at $FCE2. The installed hardware vector points one byte earlier to the RTI.
If the timer is running, update the temporary timer display and subtract twice from the main decimal counter. Set the timeout flags when the counter wraps.
Fill the five decimal digit cells with glyph $6E, leaving the punctuation cell untouched.
Decrement the low digit once before subtracting with decimal borrow across the five displayed digits. Skip the separator and reset the display when it underflows.
Subtract one at the whole-unit end of the screen's decimal timer. Borrow across the three high digits and report underflow by returning $FF.
Delay counter for the two-digit pickup timer. The interrupt reloads it with $1E when it decrements a displayed unit.
Write the glyphs for the initial temporary timer value and put colour byte $09 in both cells.
When sprite-enable bit 1 is set, alternate the effect counter and decrement the two item-timer digits at intervals. On underflow, blank the timer and clear the enable bit.
Replace both temporary timer digits with blank glyph zero.
Zero byte between the timer clearing helper and control polling entry.

Read port 2 on $DC00 with the matrix deselected. Scan five keyboard input bits and combine their mask with the active-low joystick sample at $6B. The held keyboard flags can only clear bits in that sample.
Zero means no pending edge update. The raster dispatch selects $1400 for positive and $1423 for negative values.
Select the round's palette and character set, then expand the first 40 terrain metatiles to the playfield.
Scratch for calculating six times the selected palette index.
Use the round index in $1E to select an eight-page terrain glyph bank and a six-byte palette. Populate both raster palettes, copy the glyphs, and select the matching character colour page.
Sixteen byte pairs. The first byte chooses a six-byte palette at $1186 and the second selects a terrain glyph bank and character colour page.
Second byte in the round palette and tileset pair. The first entry uses terrain bank zero.
Four six-byte palettes. Each holds background and two common colours for the upper and lower terrain sections, in that order.
Second byte in each six-byte landscape palette, used in the upper landscape at $D022.
Third palette byte, set in $D023 for the upper landscape.
Fourth palette byte, stored as the background for the lower terrain raster phase.
Fifth palette byte, set in $D022 near the bottom of the landscape.
Sixth palette byte in each of the four presets, used as the lower landscape value for $D023.
Set $20/$21 to $9800 plus 256 times the terrain bank number in $1F.
Copy $800 bytes from the terrain bank at $E000 plus $800 times the bank index stored in $1F. The VIC reads this copy at $7000.
Compute the stage map address as $9C00 plus $140 times the zero-based round index and draw the first 40 tile IDs.
Character index into the selected four-row group, advanced by one within each tile row and by 37 across the row boundary.
Source byte in the sixteen-cell metatile currently being expanded.
Convert the tile ID in A to an address in $B000. Using Y as the metatile's position, draw its 16 character codes in four rows and colour each through the current 256-entry palette.
Multiply the A register's tile ID by sixteen and add $B000. Return the little-endian definition address in $08/$09.

Ignore directional commands in the death pose or when the scroll lock is set. Test the nearby ground cell and the active-low stick, then request the relevant signed scroll direction or turn the player and update their pose.
On a transition into negative scroll, prefetch left-edge tiles and turn the sprite toward that direction before selecting a pose.
Fine-scroll phase counter. Four two-pixel adjustments transfer a whole screen column.
Zero holds the screen. The raster selects different shifts for positive and negative values.

On the first three ticks of the four-tick scroll sequence, add two to the low three bits of the horizontal VIC scroll. On the fourth tick, shift the generated screen and colour columns right and signal the edge-column work.
Shift the final two landscape character and colour rows right after the earlier rows have moved. Clear the pending edge-draw flag.
Move the final two landscape character and colour rows left and clear the pending edge-draw flag.
Variant that shifts only the row starting at $46F8 to the right, together with its colours.
Variant that shifts only the row starting at $46F8 to the left, together with its colours.
Move the fine scroll two pixels in the other direction. When crossing a cell boundary, shift the generated landscape left, advance the map column and set the right-edge draw flag.
Refill the four pending tile pointers at a metatile boundary. Read the required character column from each tile definition and write the cells and colours at the right edge of the landscape.
Advance the map position for this edge update, refresh tile pointers when needed, and write a character column and colours at the opposite edge of the landscape.
Compute the round map pointer adjusted by the scroll position. Expand the four tile IDs for the incoming right-hand column and check the corresponding column's event byte.
Read the four tile IDs at the map's left edge, convert them to definition addresses and inspect the corresponding column's event byte.
Call the SID update and service it once more if the coarse-scroll flag is set, then clear that flag.

Begin the round transition when the required scroll position is reached. Freeze scrolling, show the round summary, increment the round index and branch to the final message when the new index reaches 16.
Retained zero byte between the round state handler and the bonus-screen setup.
Clear active objects and restore the lettering graphics and palette. Draw the bonus panel, then increment the visible round number with decimal carry and reset the displayed timer to 100.
Copy the first $578 bytes of the static glyph set at $7800 into the terrain character buffer at $7000 for title and message displays.
Draw four 13-character bonus labels from $1844 onward at fixed positions, converting their letters to panel glyphs with colour byte $09. Then copy the six timer cells into the second line.
Four 13-byte fields for the round bonus panel, holding the repulse, bonus rank, timer and bonus total labels.
Second fixed-width label in the bonus panel, printed on the row below the repulse count.
Third fixed-width label, written beside the remaining-time award.
Fourth fixed-width label, written beside the sum of the round's bonuses.
Fill 26 consecutive cells in each of four rows with screen code $F9 for the summary display.
Four zero bytes separate the row-fill helper from the next row of stored tile codes.
Forty terrain glyph IDs forming a patterned border row. The eight inner groups repeat $FE,$FA,$FA,$FB and the outer groups use $FD,$FC,$FA,$FB.
Loop counter initialised with the zero-based round number. The bonus tally runs until this decrement goes negative.
Count repulsed objects in 100-point steps, then add the round rank bonus in 1000-point steps and the remaining timer in 100-point steps. Animate the running total before transferring it to the score.
Preserve X and Y while a nested countdown from $64 and $32 adds a delay between characters and bonus ticks.

Freeze play, clear the temporary timer and start the end sequence. Move the two scene sprites unless the final round is complete, then compare scores, accept qualifying initials and wait for the restart input.
Offset into the three editable initials in the top panel.
Initialise three initials to A. Left and right step through the alphabet for the highlighted cell, and fire commits it. Copy the score and initials to a record and reorder the score table.
Fill the 16 playfield rows at $44A0 through $471F with blank character zero.
Wait for a press and release of the active-low fire bit, start tune four, and wait for the driver to signal completion at $812D.
Display the fire prompt and keyboard legend on the screen, using the font converter and colour byte $09. Repaint while fire is released. On press, replace the legend with the story.
Line inviting the player to press fire. The renderer stops at the high-bit terminator before the F1 line.
F1 pause mapping, rendered at $454A until a high-bit terminator.
F3 reset mapping, rendered at $4572 until a high-bit terminator.
F5 sound mapping, rendered at $459A until a high-bit terminator.
Z for left movement and Return for fire, rendered together on one row.
X for right movement and Shift for jump, rendered on the row below the left and fire mappings.
Space for crouch, rendered below the jump mapping.
Final line offering a joystick as an alternative to the keyboard.
Translate a stored display byte into the custom character set. Space becomes zero and period becomes $79. The arithmetic maps ASCII A to $54 and zero to $6E.

Clear the landscape and type the prologue from $1E7A, copying glyph and colour one cell at a time with a delay. A high-bit control either advances two screen rows or ends the message and waits for fire.
Print the end message from $1F5B with the same paced glyph and colour writes as the story, then wait for a fresh fire press.
Wait while fire is held and then while it is released, using bit 4 of the sampled controls. Return on the next press.
Eight story lines about successive rulers, read until $FE. Other high-bit separators advance the next line by two screen rows.
Congratulatory text printed after the final round. High-bit line controls separate lines and $FE ends the message.
Twenty-one small vertical deltas read backwards for ascent and forwards for falling. The fall routine clamps its index at $13.

Walk eight object records starting at $4340 and put their coordinates, colour, and shape pointer in VIC order. Use the mirrored shape slot when the record is flagged, then write the assembled high X bits.
Shift six non-player objects by two pixels with the displayed terrain. A positive scroll request adds to their X values and a negative one subtracts, with carry or borrow into the high X byte.
Add or subtract a horizontal displacement for the object selected by X. Preserve its separate high X byte when the low-byte arithmetic crosses a page.
Eight-byte strides that convert object slot indices to byte offsets in the record array.
Zero permits a new attack. Negative values hold orientation and raised-attack flags. One waits for fire to release.
Attack countdown and index into the raised weapon offsets.
Index into the player vertical delta sequence. Decrement while rising and advance when falling.
Start an attack on fire when the round and pose permit it, choosing a horizontal or raised attack from the up bit. Track its duration and location until the attack finishes and fire is released.
Set the weapon phase to waiting for release, clear its two-byte software X coordinate and write zero to the hardware sprite 7 Y register.

Twelve coordinate pairs for the raised attack. The first byte goes directly to sprite X and the second is subtracted from the player's Y. The direction selects whether the countdown index is used forwards or backwards.
Y component of the first offset pair. The raised attack subtracts this component from the player's Y and clamps the result.
Move the death sprite horizontally and through its up-and-down arc, then clear the active powers and reset the timer and object state. If a life remains, restore the player at the visible terrain.
Dispatch on Rygar's pose for jumping, falling, crouching or dying. Up without attack begins ascent. The screen cell below the player determines the falling transition and where landing stops it.
Counts down to the next walking frame and is reloaded according to the player's state.
Cycle shape IDs $33 through $38 for walking, with a slower delay during a round transition. Pose and attack state choose the alternatives outside a walk.
Choose a stationary, crouched or attack shape according to pose and attack flags. Leave the death pose to its own animation.
Accumulates the low-pair bits during bit-table generation and holds the intermediate opacity mask.
Holds the reversed middle pixel pair masked with $0C.
Receives the leading pixel pair during table construction.
Build the 256-entry multicolour-pixel reversal table at $9200 and the 256-entry opaque-pixel mask at $9300. The lookup removes repeated bit arithmetic from sprite rendering.
A is a source shape pointer relative to the VIC bank at $4000. Use the lookup table to reverse every four-pixel byte and exchange the first and third bytes of each of the 21 rows in the destination.
Preserves the current sprite-record index across the bitmap reversal routine.
Offset in the mirrored-shape destination table.
Check the displayed shape for each hardware sprite. Regenerate the mirrored copy if its flag is set and the shape differs from the cache.
Current VIC slot plus eight for indexing the list of cached source shapes.
Sixteen bank-relative $40-separated slots at offsets $3C00 through $3FC0. Mirroring adds $4000 to the selected offset.
High byte of the first bank-relative sprite mirror offset, addressed at the same even index as its low byte.
Trigger the death pose if Rygar has fallen or a hazard flag is set. Disable the displayed player sprites, set the animation countdown, preserve direction and decrement the lives counter.
For a lives value below four, use it to blank one group of three cells on each row of the lower panel.
Offset within the new life icon's three cells in each row.
For a count below five, redraw the new icon with three successive glyphs per row, starting with $A5, $A8 and $AB.
Cached high X bits transferred to $D010 for the landscape sprites.
Reuse sprites 0 through 4 near the bottom of the screen. Set their Y coordinate to $D8 and take their five X and shape pairs from $261E.
Five X-coordinate and shape-pointer pairs for the bottom-row power icons.
Shape pointer used for the first power icon.
Horizontal coordinate of the second power icon.
Sprite bitmap pointer for the second power icon.
Horizontal coordinate of the centre power icon.
Sprite bitmap pointer for the centre power icon.
Horizontal coordinate of the fourth power icon.
Sprite bitmap pointer for the fourth power icon.
Horizontal coordinate of the last power icon.
Sprite bitmap pointer for the last power icon.
Convert the object type in A to a two-byte score increment. Queue an effect, stop the attack unless a power flag permits it to continue, and add the points to the current score.
Little-endian point increments indexed by object type through $2628.
High score byte paired with the low byte at $2660, selected at a stride of two.
Clear the first 14 object records and the status, animation and position arrays used to draw them.
Call the nested busy delay twenty times while preserving the countdown in X.
If the lives count is zero, stop the scroll, clear active objects and enter the game-over handler.
Convert the selected object's X and Y pixel coordinates to a landscape screen-cell pointer in $31/$32 for terrain tests.
Inspect the column ten metatiles ahead of the current scroll position.
Use zero lookahead for the incoming left edge. Test the current event flags and set the pending enemy type when the scroll is aligned with a metatile boundary.
Use the player's position and the current map offset to look up the column event. If the pickup flag is set, clear it and derive a replacement tile and target screen position.
Low byte patched into the map lookup at $27AB.
The high byte patched into the $27AB load after adding the rounded scroll position and the round's map offset. Its handover value is a placeholder.
Low address byte in the replacement tile load.
High byte of the source operand patched into the tile redrawing loop after multiplying the tile ID by sixteen.
Low address byte in the patched screen cell store.
Patched screen page in the metatile replacement loop.
Low address byte in the patched colour RAM store.
Patched colour RAM page in the metatile replacement loop.
Search slots 13 down to 8 for a free entry. Use the event-group table and existing powers to choose a pickup and fill its flags, shape, colour and position.
Use the captured VIC collision bits, the weapon and player positions, and the object state arrays to test contact. Convert a hit to points and an effect or collect a power, time or life pickup.
Increment the hit counters, select the reaction direction from the object's X coordinate, add the type's points, then clear the object type and start its disappearance counter.
Step the pointer by eight bytes and loop through objects 4 to 13 before checking contact against the player's body.
Scan the active object records and apply X and Y bounds to the candidates named by the VIC collision mask. A negative object type is a collectible and its index selects effects in $2C47.
Sixteen screen offsets for replacing a metatile in place, arranged as four runs of four adjacent cells on rows forty columns apart.
Selects the placement branch and offsets the index into the collectible type table.
Difference between the rounded metatile position and the current scroll. Added to the screen base for the pickup replacement.
Scratch for the event column index and later temporary object-slot storage.
Copy of $D01E from the panel IRQ. Contacts test a mask before checking object bounds.
Counter advanced from the collision routine and used to index pickup selection.
VIC collision bit associated with each software object slot for candidate filtering.
Map the varying pickup selector to the type placed in a free slot. Skip powers already present except when the selected type is three.
Four type codes cycled by repeated hits on the cycling collectible.
Four-way selection counter incremented when the cycling collectible changes.
Hit counter whose low two bits decide when to select the next type.
Sprite colour for each of eleven collectible types.
Shape pointer for each of the same eleven collectible types.
Per-type power and effect bits. The collection routine ORs the low five bits into the player's powers.
Little-endian map base adjustment per round for locating a collectable's replacement metatile.
High byte of the first pickup map offset. The per-round lookup uses the same doubled index for both bytes.
Offset of the score or bonus field being converted or updated.
Three-byte candidate score compared and moved through the high-score table.
Candidate score byte at weight 256.
Candidate byte of greatest weight, compared first when sorting.
Ten three-byte ranked numeric scores that the sorter compares next to the candidate buffer.
Current three-byte score, updated through $2D67 and converted for the upper panel.
Middle byte of the player's current score. Receives carries from the low byte.
High byte of current score, used in the qualification comparison.
Three independent 24-bit sums for repulse count, rank and remaining time, initialised in the bonus tally.
Three-byte total shown in the summary and transferred to the current score in units of 100.
Middle byte of the summary total, borrowed through when the tally subtracts 100.
High byte of the summary total. The next three bytes separate the total from the candidate initials.
Three initials for the score currently being inserted, stored as custom glyph IDs.
Second of the three encoded letters entered on the high-score screen.
Third candidate initial, copied from the third editable screen cell.
The ranked initials next to the candidate's. The sorter moves three glyphs together and advances the records by four bytes.
Nonzero when the last sort pass swapped two records and needs a further pass.
Byte offset used when swapping adjacent records' initials.
Compare adjacent three-byte scores most-significant byte first. Swap score and initials together when the lower record ranks higher, repeating passes until no swap is needed.
Low byte of the value to add to the selected score field.
Middle byte of the pending score addition.
High byte of the pending score addition.
Index relative to $2C73 selecting the field receiving the addition.
Add a 24-bit increment to the selected score or bonus field and refresh the unpacked decimal digits.
Read a 24-bit number selected by X in the score area and divide by ten repeatedly. Convert the remainders to eight screen digit codes at $2DD8.
Eight unpacked decimal glyphs written right to left by repeated division.
Low byte of the working sum written back into the chosen score field.
Middle byte of the working score sum.
High byte of the working sum after propagating the carry.
Target column used to render a number or glyph string.
Target row index passed to the screen row pointer helper.
Nonzero means to keep digit zero visible even before a significant digit has appeared.
Index of the first digit in the number buffer to render.
Colour written to each cell of the rendered decimal field.
Use the caller's panel row, column, colour and starting digit to render a decimal field. A zero flag allows leading zero glyphs to become blanks.
Write a glyph string from $66/$67 to a screen row and column with the requested colour. End at $FF or when the byte index wraps.
Numeric-record offset decremented by three as the high-score table is drawn.
Working column for the high-score heading and numeric scores. Initials use their own fixed column.
Current screen row for the next high-score output.
Render the score records beneath the table heading, with a numeric score and three stored initials per row.
Low byte of the number to divide, replaced by the low quotient byte.
Middle dividend byte, overwritten with the middle quotient byte.
High dividend byte, overwritten with the high quotient byte.
Low byte shifted by the restoring division before it is copied to $2EDF.
Receives the carries from the lower byte when shifting the working quotient.
Working quotient's highest byte in the 24-bit divider.
Divisor value ten subtracted or restored during decimal conversion.
Shift one bit per iteration through a 24-bit unsigned division. Use $2EE5 as the divisor and return the quotient in $2EDF through $2EE1.
Two ascending four-byte sequences. The first starts at one and advances by ten, and the second starts at one and advances by nine.
Byte $14 following the two runs of increasing values.
Four-pass countdown used to throttle score display updates.
Reload a four-pass divider and render the current score digits in the upper panel when it expires.
If $69 selects a message, clear the old cells, print up to thirteen characters from the selected pointer in $2FB7 and mark the message handled.
Blank the thirteen upper-panel cells starting at $4443.
Little-endian pointers used by the top-panel message renderer at $2F69.
High byte of the first message pointer, read at the same doubled message index.
First stored upper-panel status string selected by the pointer table at $2FB7.
Upper-panel game-over text selected when the end sequence queues message one.
Third status string in the same upper-panel message selection.
Fourth upper-panel status string, queued after all five power bits are set.
Round 1 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 5 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 2 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 3 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 3 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 3 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 4 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 1 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 5 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 1 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 6 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 0 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 7 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 2 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 8 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 2 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 9 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 0 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 10 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 2 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 11 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 1 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 12 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 0 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 13 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 2 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 14 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 0 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 15 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 0 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 16 event bytes for the 80 terrain columns. Of these, 0 have the low bit set when copied. The upper six bits provide the pending object code and the low bits carry pickup-related flags.
Round 1 initial object queue, copied to $43E0 in reverse order. The eight stored object codes are $01, $00, $03, $02, $04, $00, $02, $04.
Round 2 initial object queue, copied to $43E0 in reverse order. The eight stored object codes are $02, $02, $00, $02, $01, $01, $08, $09.
Round 3 initial object queue, copied to $43E0 in reverse order. The eight stored object codes are $19, $09, $08, $1A, $08, $09, $08, $08.
Round 4 initial object queue, copied to $43E0 in reverse order. The eight stored object codes are $0E, $0D, $0E, $0D, $0E, $0D, $0E, $06.
Round 5 initial object queue, copied to $43E0 in reverse order. The eight stored object codes are $01, $00, $01, $00, $01, $00, $01, $00.
Round 6 initial object queue, copied to $43E0 in reverse order. The eight stored object codes are $09, $08, $09, $08, $09, $08, $09, $08.
Round 7 initial object queue, copied to $43E0 in reverse order. The eight stored object codes are $0E, $0D, $0E, $0D, $18, $17, $18, $17.
Round 8 initial object queue, copied to $43E0 in reverse order. The eight stored object codes are $01, $00, $06, $00, $01, $06, $00, $06.
